PRODUCT VISION · NOT A DRUG ASSAY

Test ideas earlier.
Learn from biology.

We're building simulations that let drug teams test ideas on a computer before running them in the lab.

Synthetic demo. It does not predict drug effects or replace clinical trials.

Details

Drug development can take more than a decade and billions of dollars. We aim to test candidate drugs and therapies earlier in progressively validated biological simulations, helping teams prioritize laboratory work. This demo tests one piece of that vision: whether timed changes in cell-to-cell communication can redirect a regenerating body plan. Future models would need experimental voltage, anatomy, and molecular measurements, plus held-out validation, before they could support drug decisions.

CUSTOMERS

Teams building biology

Pharma and biotech developers, and AI companies extending their models into living systems.

A planned service for candidate therapies in selected biological scenarios, with a future privacy-preserving option for proprietary inputs and model details.

DATA PRODUCTS

Measured context

Potentially licensed datasets on morphogenesis and intervention responses, including cell-culture and organoid scenarios.

GROWTH

Improve, then scale

Refine measurement and validation, retrain on new time series, then expand simulation quality, scope, and throughput.

How private studies might work

We would explore confidential or encrypted computation so partners could limit disclosure of candidate details while protecting model internals. This is a proposed design, not a feature of the current demo. Zero-knowledge proofs alone do not run a hidden-input biological simulation; the privacy architecture would need separate design and security review.

Start with a testable question.

The first prospective users are research teams in biotech and pharma. The next step is a narrow study: agree on one biological question, compare predictions with measured results, and show where the model succeeds or fails before offering it for research decisions.

01 / EARLY ADOPTERS

AI is already in the lab.

Benchling's 2026 survey of about 100 biotech and biopharma organizations already using AI describes demand for scientific tools alongside persistent data and validation gaps. Its sample represents AI adopters, not the entire industry.

02 / RESEARCH WORKFLOW

Validation defines the use.

NCATS tissue-chip collaborations and IQ MPS Affiliate reports show pharma, researchers, and technology developers working on fit-for-purpose models and adoption. They are category precedents, not tests of this simulation.

03 / FUTURE ROUTE

Qualification takes evidence.

The FDA accepted a different AI digital liver model's letter of intent into ISTAND. That is the first of three qualification steps, not approval of that tool or this one.

Proposed sequence: research collaboration → held-out experimental validation → scoped simulation studies and measured-data products.

The computer research checkpoint and this live browser demo are separate models. The demo combines 254 learned values with explicit synthetic rules, applied across a 32 × 32 grid. It does not load or compress the research checkpoint's 50,741 weights.

01 / INTERACTIVE PROTOCOL

Grow. Cut. Change communication.

Every view reads the same evolving tissue state. The normal target is a reference image only; it is never supplied to the model during inference.

How to run this demo 4 quick steps
  1. Develop normal. Let the precursor grow to one head and one tail, then click Cut trunk.
  2. Choose a condition. Untreated, brief, half-dose, and sustained broad blocks each restart from the same saved trunk fragment. A condition runs through treatment and washout automatically.
  3. Watch the three layers. Anatomy shows organs; electrical state shows signed synthetic voltage (red positive, blue negative); the third panel shows regulatory, axis, and structural fields. Choose Observe speed or use Pause and Step 1 to inspect timing.
  4. Test persistence. After sustained broad block finishes, click Clean recut to regrow the treated tissue without another block. Use Reset to start over.

All durations are simulation ticks, not calibrated biological hours. These are synthetic outcomes, not predictions for real octanol doses.

RESEARCH CHECKPOINT / FATE DIAGNOSTIC

Separate cues for separate fates.

This 50,741-weight research-model diagnostic compares a normal target with a learned state at update 128. Distinct anatomy, head, eye, tail, and biochemical views gave the model clearer synthetic targets. It is separate from the live 254-value browser protocol.

A memory of signals.
A choice of anatomy.

The tissue state tracks physical matter, synthetic voltage, biochemical activity, regulatory and axis fields, structure, fast and slow edge memory, delayed communication, and induction memory. A cut removes cells and their incident connections while preserving the state of surviving tissue.

Technical details

The computer research checkpoint has 50,741 learned weights and is preserved separately. The live browser experiment runs a different 254-parameter recurrent rule across 1,024 cells. Those learned values work alongside explicit synthetic dynamics; they are not a conversion of the research checkpoint's weights.

The v3 transition starts from the original 254-parameter protocol checkpoint. Its separate candidate checkpoint changes two scalar weights by manual calibration; explicit synthetic rules govern wound growth, an axial chart retained in cells, a wound-conditioned voltage response to coupling loss, organizer thresholds, eye placement, and fast-to-slow connection consolidation. The voltage response begins during treatment, and prior voltage participates in the later induction-memory update. Organizer activity inhibits posterior tail commitment as a new head emerges. The browser runs a JavaScript port of the recurrent transition; no Python service or synthetic teacher is called during inference.

The three panels show one current state, including regulatory, polarity, and structural channels separately selectable in the third panel. The body and inherited axis exist at the cut; the timing test concerns the new posterior response after treatment. The target reference is displayed for comparison only.

What the demo shows.
What it cannot claim.

↗

Normal control

The intact precursor develops a normal synthetic one-head, one-tail planarian. A trunk fragment can regenerate under untreated and brief-block conditions.

SYNTHETIC DEMO
↗

Sustained broad block

In the tested Python protocol, sustained middle-band broad coupling block creates a posterior organizer that survives washout and a clean recut. The brief and half-dose protocols are negative controls.

TESTED PROTOCOL
○

Biological interpretation

The early local voltage shift and deterministic two-head outcome are synthetic modeling assumptions. Tick durations are uncalibrated. These outputs do not validate a drug response or predict real planarian regeneration.

LIMITATION

In the protocol timing test, the treatment-associated posterior voltage shift began during the coupling block, before the measured regulatory difference and visible posterior head. View validation details ↗

PLANNED AUTONOMOUS DATA PIPELINE

Measure voltage.
Read gene programs.

We plan to pair embedded bioelectronics with genetically encoded voltage indicators (GEVIs) or voltage-sensitive dyes (VSDs), then connect those electrical time series to transcriptomic measurements from matched samples and time points.

01CaptureEmbedded electrodes and GEVI or VSD imaging
→
02ProfileExport transcriptomic data from matched samples
→
03LearnAlign, train, and validate on held-out interventions

Automating this loop could grow the quality and range of future simulations. It has not been built for this demo. Experimental precedents include embedded organoid electronics, GEVI imaging, planarian VSDs, and transcriptomic export.

DESIGN ITERATION / SYNTHETIC SNAPSHOTS

Distinct signals made learning clearer.

A key design choice was to give head, eye, tail, and biochemical fates more differentiated synthetic signatures. Even the research checkpoint's 50,741 weights make it a small model, so clear cues mattered. These snapshots show the move from mixed posterior responses to a clearer sustained-block and clean-recut contrast; they do not establish biological validity or success rates.
